questions.question: Set out the purpose and questions of an investigation into real headgear, the kinds of source that may be used and how each is recorded, and the contents of the comparison table and the closing list.
questions.expected_answer: The purpose is to understand how real headgear lift loads safely so that the team's design is informed by what works; the questions ask how the rope is driven, what the structure looks like and why, how people and ore are carried, what stops a falling cage, what materials and sections are used, and what has changed over time. Sources include photographs, which can be scaled from a known object and are recorded with mine, place and date; drawings and diagrams from textbooks, safety publications and museums; visits where a headgear is within reach; interviews with current or former mine workers recorded with name, role, date and permission; and written sources summarised in the team's words with the source noted. The record has an annotated page per headgear and a table comparing three to five by location, mine and mineral, approximate height, structural form, winder type, number of ropes, conveyance and year, and ends with a list of features the team will borrow with the reason for each.

questions.question: Describe the four main parts of a wire-rope winding system, distinguish a drum winder from a friction winder and the headgear form each tends to use, and list the safety features required by law.
questions.expected_answer: The winder on the surface drives the rope; the steel wire rope of twisted strands around a core, typically 40 to 60 millimetres in diameter, combines tensile strength with the flexibility to bend over a sheave; the grooved sheave wheel at the top of the headgear turns the rope from horizontal to vertical and carries its full tension; the conveyance, a cage for people or a skip for ore, hangs on the rope. A drum winder winds the rope onto a cylindrical drum through a gearbox, often two drums on one shaft wound in opposite senses so conveyances balance, and because the drum stores all the rope it suits a steel A-frame headgear with a back-leg towards the winder house. A friction or Koepe winder passes several ropes over a driven wheel gripped by friction, with a conveyance on each end and a tail rope for balance, and is usually mounted on top of a concrete tower over the shaft for very deep shafts. The law requires daily rope inspection and scheduled replacement, brakes that apply automatically on power failure or overspeed, overwind and underwind devices, safety catches on cages that grip the guides if the rope breaks, arrester gear at the shaft ends, and depth indicators and signalling systems.

questions.question: Describe the three structural forms of headgear and why each stands, list the features a team should borrow for a model with the reason for each, and outline how headgear have changed since the 1880s.
questions.expected_answer: The steel A-frame has a triangulated tower over the shaft carrying the sheave platform, with back-legs sloping to the ground towards the winder house that take the rope's horizontal pull as compression; the four-legged tower is a square braced tower without a back-leg used where the winder is close or two winders balance; the concrete tower is a reinforced concrete structure with the friction winder on top, strong through its material and closed section with rope loads carried internally. Features to borrow: triangulation in every face against sway; a back-leg or brace towards the model winder, since the motor pulls the top towards itself; a wide anchored base against toppling; a grooved sheave on an axle on a beam spanning the tower; taut guides down the shaft so the cage rises straight and a catch can grip; a brake lever or pawl on the drum shaft; a bumper under the sheave beam as an overwind stop; and a pointer on the drum shaft as a depth indicator, each recorded with its source and reason. Headgear were timber in the 1880s Witwatersrand, steel by 1900 with the A-frame form settled by the 1930s, and concrete towers with friction winders appeared from the 1950s for deep Free State and West Wits shafts, driven by depth, load and safety law.
